questions.question: Why should functions usually return values instead of only printing?
options: Printing is not allowed in Python.
Returned values are easier to test and reuse.
Return statements make code run in parallel.
Printing changes the type of the value.
questions.explanation: A returned value can be captured, passed to another function, or checked in a test; a printed string vanishes to the console and cannot be inspected or reused programmatically.

questions.question: What problem can `def add_item(item, items=[])` cause?
options: The default list is shared across calls and can retain old values.
Python does not allow lists as defaults.
The function will always return an empty list.
The function cannot accept more than one argument.
questions.explanation: Mutable defaults like lists are created once when the function is defined, not fresh on each call; successive calls share the same list object, so previous appends accumulate unexpectedly.

questions.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: Parameters are always strings.
They are the same thing.
Arguments are only keyword values.
A parameter is in the function definition; an argument is the value passed at call time.
questions.explanation: Parameters are placeholder names declared in the def statement; arguments are the actual values supplied when you call the function — the two terms describe the same slot from different perspectives.

questions.question: What does `*args` do in a function signature?
options: Prevents default arguments.
Collects keyword arguments into a dictionary.
Collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
Requires all arguments to be keyword-only.
questions.explanation: *args gathers any extra positional arguments beyond the named parameters into a tuple; **kwargs does the equivalent for keyword arguments into a dictionary — they are distinct.

questions.question: What does a function return if there is no return statement?
options: An empty string
None
It raises NameError.
questions.explanation: Python implicitly returns None when execution falls off the end of a function without a return statement; beginners often mistake this for returning the last assigned variable, which it is not.

questions.question: Why can keyword arguments improve readability?
options: They force Python to infer types.
They run faster than positional arguments.
They prevent defaults from being used.
They make argument intent explicit at call sites.
questions.explanation: Writing process(timeout=30, retry=True) is self-documenting; positional process(30, True) forces readers to look up the signature to understand what each value means.

questions.question: When should you split a function into smaller functions?
options: When the function has exactly one parameter.
When one function handles multiple unrelated responsibilities.
When the function uses return.
Never; larger functions are always better.
questions.explanation: A function that does multiple unrelated things is hard to name accurately, test in isolation, and reuse; extracting each responsibility into its own function makes each piece easier to reason about.

questions.question: What is the main value of a docstring?
options: It explains behavior and usage for humans and tools.
It turns dynamic typing into static typing.
It makes code execute faster.
It replaces tests.
questions.explanation: A docstring is readable by help(), IDEs, and doc generators; it communicates what the function does, what arguments it expects, and what it returns — none of which speed up execution or replace tests.
